newsitem.title: FRANCE: Juppe allies air misgivings before confidence vote.
newsitem.headline: Juppe allies air misgivings before confidence vote.

text.p: French Prime Minister Alain Juppe's coalition partners voiced renewed doubts on Wednesday about his presentational skills and some of his policies but promised to back the government in a parliamentary confidence vote.

The opposition Socialist party said the vote would be hollow since the government controlled 480 of the 577 National Assembly seats, and would not reflect the confidence of French voters, who were demanding a fundamental change of policy.

Gilles de Robien, floor leader of the UDF party, junior partner in the centre-right coalition, said Juppe had to do a better job of explaining policy and expressed doubts about a proposed new anti-racism law and electoral reform.
He told Radio Monte Carlo his group would back the confidence motion later on Wednesday because the government's "economic, fiscal and social policies go exactly in the direction sought by the UDF".

But he added: "I feel like telling the prime minister that with a bit more explanation...and a bit more consultation, I am sure the climate would be better and the French people would naturally be more satisfied."

Juppe's public approval rating is close to an all-time low at just 30 percent and President Jacques Chirac has been forced to intervene twice in the last week to shield him from criticism within the ruling coalition.
With the economy stagnant and unemployment at a record 12.6 percent and still rising, the prime minister was expected to plead for patience and perseverance in his policy speech.

De Robien said UDF members of parliament were fed up with learning from the media about Juppe policy initiatives such as a proposal to add an element of proportional representation to the parliamentary election system, or a plan to toughen legislation against racist statements.

"The prime minister and the government are proposing bills...that are not the priority today. Who cares about the voting system for electing deputies? Do the French people care? We don't think so," he said.

For the first time in months, there was also talk of Chirac possibly using his constitutional right to dissolve parliament and call an early general election rather than letting the legislature run its course till March 1998.
Regional Development Minister Jean-Claude Gaudin said in a radio interview the coalition should be prepared in case Chirac decided to call a snap parliamentary election.
"The decision depends solely on the president and I don't think he has confided in many people on that subject. In any case, not in me," Gaudin told Europe-1.
But he added: "If it takes place early, that is all the more reason for us first to be ready, second to be determined and third to be perfectly united."

The newspaper Le Monde said Chirac had discussed with UDF leader Francois Leotard the idea of bringing the election forward, although he had appeared to rule it out on July 14, saying on television that dissolution was not a weapon of convenience and could only be used if there were a political crisis.

Despite Juppe's unpopularity, such a move might enable the coalition to win re-election with a greatly reduced majority, since the opposition Socialists are still discredited in the eyes of many voters and have not yet adopted a new platform.
That would ensure Chirac had a parliamentary majority for the rest of his seven-year term, rather than risk having to share power with the Left from 1998.

However political analysts said leaking talk of a dissolution might just be a tactic by Chirac and Juppe to force fractious coalition parliamentarians back into line, since dozens would stand to lose their seats in any early election.
